title: Smoke from Australia's 2019–20 bushfires drifted all the way to South America
body: Australia's Black Summer fires [burnt more than 24 million hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_Australian_bushfire_season), and the worst of them, around the new year, built towering fire clouds that lifted smoke **over 10 km** up. Up there sunlight heated the soot, so the smoke kept rising on its own: within two weeks of 6 January 2020 the plume's top had climbed deep into the stratosphere, higher than any wildfire plume NASA's CALIPSO satellite had tracked before. Fast high-altitude winds then carried it east across the South Pacific to South America, and NASA expected it to [travel on around the globe back to Australia](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/global-transport-of-australian-bushfire-smoke/).

cover.alt: World map of airborne particles in a computer model, with orange dust over the Sahara and a red smear of smoke over south-eastern Australia

slides.alt: World map of airborne particles. Red, orange and white streaks of smoke pour off south-eastern Australia, stretch east across the South Pacific, reach the tip of South America and drift on into the South Atlantic.
slides.caption: NASA's computer model of particles in the air, 22 December 2019 to 28 January 2020, about 2.5 days every second. Red to white is carbon from smoke; orange is desert dust.
slides.credit: NASA Global Modeling and Assimilation Office · Public domain · excerpt

slides.question: Within two weeks of 6 January 2020, how high did the top of the smoke plume rise?
slides.explanation: About 25 km, well into the stratosphere. NASA’s CALIPSO satellite first measured the smoke at 15 to 19 km on 6 January; sunlight warming the soot kept lifting it.

slides.heading: How the smoke climbed so high

slides.label: burnt by the 2019–20 fires, from June 2019 to March 2020
slides.text: About 240,000 km². The most severe fires hit in December 2019 and January 2020.

slides.question: How much carbon monoxide did the fires push into the stratosphere, compared with British Columbia's huge 2017 fires?
slides.explanation: NASA's Aura satellite suggests about three times as much: more, in that January, than any other event it had seen outside the tropics in 15 years.
